Multi-armed bandits with arriving arms: sequential screening and reliable set maintenance Deqi Zheng ∗ Xiaoyang Xu ∗ Qiuzhen College, Tsinghua University Yuhong Yang † Yau Mathematical Sciences Center, Tsinghua University October 15, 2026 Abstract We study a stochastic multi-armed bandit problem in which new arms arrive exogenously and remain available. Performance is measured against the best currently available arm. The resulting arrival information discrepancy and drifting benchmark motivate UCB for Arriving Arms (UCB- AA), which screens new arms before they enter full competition with incumbents. We analyze this two-stage design and give a finite-budget regret analysis based on the comparisons and sample prefixes actually used. The analysis separates learning among admitted arms from delayed admission and loss of an earlier benchmark. We then ask what statistical benefit can accompany screening beyond a smaller internal active set. For simultaneous, reliable reporting of the relative near-optimal set, uncertainty about one arrival can obstruct many earlier certifications. We characterize a worst-schedule maintenance cost and identify the polynomial arrival boundary for sublinear unresolved time. A repeated-update family shows that prompt resolution of temporary membership questions can require inverse-square regret, whereas allowing more waiting admits a logarithmic upper bound. The necessary cost also holds with fixed positive probability. A separate checkpoint construction supplies attainable reporting bounds. Numerical evidence distinguishes the archived UCB-AA implementation from this construction and exposes the finite-budget cost of conservative certification. Keywords: sequential experimentation; adaptive screening; arriving arms; dynamic regret; arrival information discrepancy; drifting benchmark. 1 Introduction The classical multi-armed bandit framework assumes that the set of available actions is fixed in advance. In many modern applications, however, the action set expands over time. Precision oncology provides a representative example: as genomic profiling has advanced, the set of approved ∗ † The first two authors contributed equally. Corresponding author: yyangsc@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn. 1 Figure 1: The historical motivating illustration from the original submission: FDA approval records for targeted therapies and immunotherapies for non-small cell lung cancer over 2003–2025 (U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2025). The expanding option set motivates arriving-arm experiments. No treatment outcomes from this illustration enter the bandit simulations. targeted therapies for non-small cell lung cancer has grown substantially, so a trial designed around a fixed collection of treatments may become outdated before it is completed. Similar issues arise in online advertising and other adaptive decision problems in which new options appear sequentially. Motivated by such problems, we study the multi-armed bandit problem with arriving arms (MAB-AA). Let A t denote the set of arms available at time t, with A t ⊆ A t+1 . New arms arrive over time and remain available thereafter. Performance is evaluated against the best arm currently available, since a terminal best arm need not have been available earlier. Relative to the classical stochastic bandit setting, MAB-AA introduces two main difficulties. The first is arrival information discrepancy (AID): newly arrived arms must be explored, which repeatedly diverts samples away from well-understood incumbent arms. The second is a drifting benchmark (DB): as better arms enter the system, both the identity of the optimal arm and the regret benchmark may change over time. The setting retains stationary, unstructured reward laws and an external arrival process. Arms are not drawn on demand from a reservoir (Berry et al., 1997), and do not disappear as in mortal bandits (Chakrabarti et al., 2008). Permanent arrivals are a monotone special case of sleeping-bandit availability (Kleinberg et al., 2010). Benchmark changes are caused by new arms, rather than changes in the reward laws of existing arms as in nonstationary bandits (Besbes et al., 2014; Auer et al., 2019). Ballooning bandits already use permanent arrivals and regret against the best currently available arm (Ghalme et al., 2021); we do not claim either as a new model or comparator. From a statistical perspective, multi-armed bandit problems have long been studied as models for sequential allocation and adaptive experimentation, dating back to Robbins (1952) and the asymptotically efficient allocation theory of Lai and Robbins (1985); see also Lai (1987) for connec- tions to adaptive treatment allocation. This viewpoint has motivated a broad statistical literature, including Bayesian and index-based approaches to sequential allocation (Gittins, 1979; Berry and 2 Fristedt, 1985), response-adaptive randomization in clinical trials (Zelen, 1969; Wei and Durham, 1978; Villar et al., 2015; Williamson and Villar, 2020; Aziz et al., 2021), covariate-dependent and nonparametric bandit methods (Woodroofe, 1979; Yang and Zhu, 2002; Rigollet and Zeevi, 2010; Perchet and Rigollet, 2013), and recent high-dimensional, semiparametric, and transfer-learning formulations (Qian and Yang, 2016; Qian et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2024). These works share with ours the broad goal of learning from accumulated evidence to reduce allocation to inferior alternatives, but do not directly study the permanent exogenous arrival setting considered here. Methodologically, the two challenges call for different but complementary design principles. To address AID, our approach combines elimination steps (Even-Dar et al., 2006; Auer and Ortner, 2010; Perchet and Rigollet, 2013; Qian and Yang, 2016) with a pre-elimination mechanism tailored to the expanding action set. The key idea is to prevent the main competition stage from being repeatedly disrupted by every newly arriving arm. Instead, late arrivals are first screened against incumbent candidates, so that clearly inferior arms can be removed before receiving the full exploration budget assigned to serious contenders. To handle DB, the algorithm repeatedly updates the relevant comparison set as new arms arrive, and the analysis evaluates regret against the best arm currently available rather than against a fixed hindsight oracle. Based on these ideas, we propose UCB for Arriving Arms (UCB-AA). For UCB-AA, we derive regret upper bounds that depend explicitly on the arrival process, establish sublinear dynamic regret when arm-count growth and admission delay are controlled, study representative lower-bound regimes, and develop an online extension for unknown horizons. UCB for Arriving Arms (UCB-AA) implements this screening design. Its pre-elimination stage samples an arrival at coarse resolutions before spending the finer budget used for incumbent arms. Formal elimination then compares the merged active set. A finite-budget analysis must account for unfinished phases, arrivals waiting for admission, and any loss of a previously admitted best arm. We give that accounting explicitly and establish a sample-count bound without compressing historical gaps into a terminal gap. The active set alone does not describe what has been learned about all available arms. An excluded arm may be statistically inferior, or it may never have been admitted. This distinction leads to a further question within the same MAB-AA setting: what does it cost to maintain reliable knowledge of the complete relative near-optimal set while collecting reward? The fixed-arm version is the ALL-ε problem (Mason et al., 2020). Joint reward and identification objectives also have established precedents (Degenne et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2026; Cho et al., 2025). Our additional requirement concerns continuing reports under arrivals, with one simultaneous correctness event and a cumulative cost for unresolved arm time. Two effects of the drifting benchmark determine that cost. An uncertain new arm can block positive certification of many well-studied incumbents. A later improvement can also make a difficult earlier membership question irrelevant. We prove a common-environment broadcast lower bound and a worst-schedule maintenance bound, obtaining the polynomial arrival exponent below which sublinear regret and sublinear unresolved time are jointly possible. In a repeated-update family, prompt maintenance has matching inverse-square regret bounds at specified horizons, whereas a 3 larger constant-factor area budget admits a logarithmic regret upper bound. A fixed-probability lower bound shows that the necessary cost is not confined to rare paths. These are substantive extensions of the original regret question, rather than guarantees inferred from the size of UCB-AA’s active set. For the reporting upper bounds we use a separate checkpoint construction, CP-UCB-AA. It preserves accumulated observations but does not remove negatively reported arms from reward selec- tion. We distinguish its guarantees from those of the two-stage UCB-AA procedure. The numerical study likewise distinguishes the original archived implementation from the reporting comparisons. It retains favorable and unfavorable original observations, while showing that conservative fixed checkpoints can be impractical at moderate budgets. 2 Multi-armed bandit problem with arriving arms 2.1 Problem formulation We consider a sequential decision process over time steps t = 1, 2, . . .. Let A be the possibly infinite set of all arms. At time t only A t ⊆ A is available, where A t ⊆ A t+1 , A 1 = ̸ ∅, and K t = |A t | < ∞. For arm i, its arrival time is τ i = inf{t ≥ 1 : i ∈ A t }. Each arm has an unknown stationary reward law on [0, 1] with mean r i . Reward streams are independent across arms, and successive observations of each arm are independent and identically distributed. The arrival process is exogenous to the learner and independent of these reward streams. We state results conditional on a fixed arrival schedule unless otherwise specified. In physical-time notation, X t,i denotes the reward observed if arm i is selected at time t. A policy is a sequence π = (π t ) t≥1 of possibly randomized rules. After seeing A t , it selects I t ∈ A t using the observed history t−1 H t−1 = (A s , I s , X s,I s ) s=1 and independent randomization, and then observes X t,I t . It does not know the arm means or future arrivals. P Write N i (t) = s≤t 1{I s = i} for the cumulative number of pulls of arm i. To distinguish pull number from physical time, represent its successive potential observations by (Y i,n ) n≥1 , so that X t,I t = Y I t ,N It (t−1)+1 . Define r̂ i (n) = n 1 X Y i,s , n s=1 r ∗ (t) = max r i , i∈A t ∆ i (t) = r ∗ (t) − r i (i ∈ A t ). For an almost surely finite stopping time τ , the cumulative dynamic regret is R τ (π) = τ X t=1 4 r ∗ (t) − r I t .  At a deterministic horizon T we write R T (π), or R T when the policy is understood. It is random through the arm selections; ER T is its expectation. A definition at random τ does not assert that every deterministic-horizon bound also holds at arbitrary stopping times. Physical time t always counts actual pulls. Algorithmic rounds are indexed separately by m. 2.2 Main statistical challenges Arrival information discrepancy (AID). A first difficulty is arrival information discrepancy. With a finite sampling budget up to time T , the learner must allocate samples both to incumbent arms and to newly arriving arms whose rewards are still highly uncertain. Under continual arrivals, this repeated re-exploration can prevent the learner from concentrating pulls on the best currently available arm. Consequently, without additional regularity conditions on the arrival process, sublinear regret may be unattainable. Drifting benchmark (DB). In contrast to the classical setting where the best mean reward is fixed, the benchmark in MAB-AA is time-dependent: r ∗ (t) = max i∈A t r i . Since A t expands over time, both the identity of the best arm and the value r ∗ (t) may change when new arms arrive. Consequently, for a fixed arm i, the suboptimal gap r ∗ (t) − r i is generally time-varying (and non-decreasing in t). This drifting benchmark complicates both algorithm design and analysis, because the learner must continuously compare well-sampled incumbent arms with newly arriving arms whose estimates are still highly uncertain. 2.3 Admission and retirement in the reward account The distinction between statistical reports and reward eligibility is useful even before introducing a policy. Let A adm ⊆ A t be an admitted set and B t ⊆ A adm its nonempty reward-active subset, with t t I t ∈ B t . At every deterministic endpoint, including one inside an algorithmic round, R T = X t≤T + (max r i − r I t ) + i∈B t X X (r ∗ (t) − max r i ) t≤T ( max r i − max r i ). i∈B t adm t≤T i∈A t i∈A adm t (1) This follows by adding and subtracting the two intermediate maxima at each pull. The terms are within-active learning, admission delay, and loss of an admitted benchmark through retirement. The latter two cannot in general be identified with arrival increments alone. On a simultaneous confidence event, the revised UCB-AA comparisons preserve a best admitted arm, making the third term zero. The checkpoint construction introduced later uses B t = A adm = A t for reward selection, t so its last two terms vanish on every sample path. 3 UCB for Arriving Arms (UCB-AA) UCB-AA is an elimination-based procedure organized by rounds. Its main idea is simple: newly arriving arms are not allowed to compete immediately with well-sampled incumbent arms. Instead, 5 they are first buffered and screened at lower cost. Only those that survive this screening step enter full competition in the next stage. This design aims to reduce wasted exploration on clearly suboptimal late arrivals while preserving the ability to detect genuinely competitive new arms. 3.1 UCB-AA under a physical sampling budget UCB for Arriving Arms (UCB-AA) uses two stages of screening. At the beginning of round m, admit the buffered batch A m and form B m = C m−1 ∪ A m , where C m−1 contains the surviving incumbents. For m ≥ 2, screen the new arms in phases p = 0, . . . , m − 2 against the incumbents and the remaining new arms; only new arms can be removed. Then apply formal elimination to the merged set in phases m − 1, m. Round zero uses phase zero, and round one uses formal phases zero and one. Empty preliminary batches are no-ops. This retains the distinction between pre-elimination, which addresses arrival information discrepancy, and formal elimination after new arms have entered the main competition. Let s m be the physical start of round m. Set A 0 = A 1 and, for m ≥ 1, admit the entire buffer, S including arrivals at s m : A m = A s m \ A(m − 1), where A(m − 1) = j<m A j . Arrivals during a call are added to the buffer before the current physical action and wait for the next round. To give this procedure a fixed-budget guarantee, specify its confidence calibration, comparison data, and stopping rule. The first describes the evidence needed to reject inferior arrivals when the best arm is already available. Its static special case is a classical calibration (Lai and Robbins, 1985; Burnetas and Katehakis, 1996). The second describes successive local comparisons as the benchmark improves. Both concern regret at a deterministic physical horizon. They are separate from the reporting requirements introduced below, and are not claimed as matching converses to an upper bound evaluated at a random round-completion time. 4.1 Static arms and arriving distractors For each horizon T , fix an exogenous deterministic arrival schedule and a baseline environment ν (0) . Complete proofs appear in the supplementary material. 5 Reliable maintenance of the near-optimal set We now supplement the allocation objective with an explicit reporting objective. The reward model, available arms, and dynamic-regret comparator remain those of Section 2. Reporting a relative near-optimal set is an additional statistical task; it is not identified with UCB-AA’s active or surviving set. We use separate report notation to keep that distinction visible. 5.1 Reporting reliability and unresolved time For 0 < ε < 1, the target is G t ε = {i ∈ A t : ∆ i (t) ≤ ε}. A report partitions A t into P t , N t , V t : certified good, certified bad, and unresolved. With 0 < δ < 1/2, let E lab = {for all t : P t ⊆ G t ε ⊆ A t \ N t }. A policy is δ-reliable if P(E lab ) ≥ 1 − δ in every allowed reward environment. Positive reports may need revision after an arrival. A sound negative report remains valid because r ∗ (t) is nondecreasing. This statement refers to the model’s stationary means and permanent availability. Reliability alone permits every arm to remain unresolved. Background arrivals again have probability 0.005, with probability 0.30 of being drawn from the near-optimal component. Short-interval retained-history comparisons and best-arm-retention diagnostics are also needed. The reporting experiments below answer a different, additional question and do not replace that algorithm comparison. 8.2 Finite-budget comparisons for reliable set maintenance We examine the cost of maintaining reliable reports at an actual sampling budget, including settings in which the conservative checkpoint construction is impractical. These comparisons assess finite- budget behavior of the reporting construction, not the two-stage UCB-AA procedure. The four environments are not the separated family used for the two-endpoint theorem, and the simulations do not test its asymptotic rates. 20 8.2.1 Protocol and competing rules All rewards are Bernoulli. We fix T = 20,000, ε = .30, η = .10, and δ = .05, with eight arms by the end of each run. There are 160 independent replications per environment. Within a replication, every method receives the same potential reward stream for each arm; its nth pull of arm i reveals the same Y i,n . Thus methods share the underlying observations without being forced to take the same actions. Arrivals occur before the action, reports follow the observation, and all methods retain previous observations. The full arrival times, means, seeds, and policy definitions are saved in a single configuration file. The first environment has initial means .65, .50 and three later batches of inferior arms, so the benchmark remains constant. The second has four successive benchmark levels .45, .70, .90, .98; some earlier unresolved membership questions become obsolete when a better arm arrives. The third introduces six arms at one time, including a new best arm. The fourth ends arrivals at pull 4037 and leaves nearly 16,000 further pulls for recovery. Noninitial batches occur 36 pulls after a 100-pull admission grid, so the short-period baseline is not evaluated only at its most favorable alignment. No policy is given future arrivals, the means, or the evaluation horizon. We implement CP-UCB-AA with FIFO service every second pull at two fixed precisions. The choice ρ = .04 satisfies 2ρ < η: on the coverage event, completing all checkpoints resolves every η- separated arm. The choice ρ = .12, inherited from the implementation supplied with the theoretical development, is a coarser engineering setting. Its labels remain reliable, but it need not resolve every arm counted by the η = .10 metric. We report these choices separately. With eight arms their total checkpoint quotas are 73,083 and 8,123 pulls, respectively. The finer setting therefore cannot complete all quotas within the chosen budget. Three comparisons isolate the allocation rule while retaining the coarser checkpoint report: FIFO service every eighth pull, confidence-driven service every second pull, and full-history UCB without designated service pulls. Confidence-driven service samples the widest interval among unresolved arms and the arm with largest upper endpoint, breaking ties by sample count and then arrival order. It stops designated service when no report remains unresolved. A completed checkpoint retains its fixed interval. We also use the full-prefix confidence report from the theory with three reward or sampling rules. UCB-prefix admits every arm immediately and uses the same full-history UCB index as CP-UCB-AA. Growing-MOSS uses the anytime index s r̂ i (n) + max{log(t/(K t n)), 0} , n with infinite index at n = 0; no minimax property of the fixed-horizon MOSS algorithm is assumed for this extension. ALL-ε adaptation uses the confidence-driven service rule every second pull and UCB otherwise. It retains all history and can revise positive reports after arrivals. This is a natural adaptation of confidence-based all-good-arm sampling, not an implementation of FAREAST or (ST) 2 . A comparison with the same boundary tolerance and service requirement is needed to distinguish the mechanisms. These observations do not estimate an optimal frontier. Growing-MOSS has the smallest mean regret in all four environments, between 52.0 and 77.3, while leaving substantially larger unresolved areas. Low regret therefore provides little evidence of timely set maintenance. Conversely, the explicit service rules pay for observations of inferior arms. Reducing service from every second to every eighth pull generally reduces regret and enlarges unresolved area. Replacing FIFO by the confidence-driven checkpoint allocation does not uniformly improve either criterion; allocation and the report’s precision both matter. For Batch100-UCB we additionally record the exact decomposition into within-active regret, 24 admission delay, and loss from previous reward retirement. Its admission-delay contributions are 0, 33.92, 16.00, and 22.40 in the four environments. No historical-retirement deficit occurred in these runs. The largest discrepancy between total regret and the sum of the three recorded components was below 3.1 × 10 −12 . The corresponding admission and retirement terms are identically zero for the methods that admit every arm immediately and retain every arm for reward selection. This accounting avoids attributing every loss outside within-active learning to arrival delay. There were no incorrect positive or negative reports in any of the 5760 runs. For one fixed environment and method, zero failures in 160 replications gives a one-sided 95% upper confidence bound of 0.0186 on its failure probability. This finite set of diagnostics does not establish the uniform, all-environment reliability guarantee. Nor do these small eight-arm experiments validate the asymptotic lower bounds, resolve the critical logarithmic gap, or establish checkpoint optimality. They show the practical cost of the conservative quotas and the importance of comparing retained- history methods under both regret and maintenance criteria. 9 Discussion We studied stochastic multi-armed bandits with arriving arms, where the available action set expands and performance is measured against the best currently available arm. Arrival information discrepancy and a drifting benchmark create repeated learning costs even though every arm has a stationary reward law. The two-stage UCB-AA design addresses the information imbalance by screening arrivals before full competition with incumbents. The revised regret account separates learning, admission delay, and loss of an earlier admitted benchmark. Its finite-budget guarantee is conditional on the stated calibration and retains the admission-delay term explicitly. The additional maintenance analysis makes precise a statistical question that the original active- set comparison left open. A smaller internal set does not establish reliable knowledge of the complete near-optimal set. One uncertain arrival can obstruct many earlier certifications, and a drifting benchmark can make difficult unresolved questions expire. The broadcast and repeated-update results characterize costs arising from these two effects. Their assumptions, including the restricted update family and the different allowed area budgets, are part of the conclusions. The worst area lower bound already occurs in a static initial batch; the temporary-task results supply a separate dynamic mechanism. UCB-AA and CP-UCB-AA serve different purposes in this analysis. The former retains the original screening architecture. The latter is a constructive reporting rule whose service precision is fixed in advance and whose unconditional reward analysis does not require correct reports. Its conservative checkpoints may be ineffective at moderate budgets, and its numerical cost is not uniformly competitive. Neither a negative report nor a smaller reported set is treated as a reduction in total storage. The supplement supplies full proofs of the quantile lower bound in Section 7 and the compatible- window truncation result. It also gives eventual exact classification by a separate revisable mul- tiresolution construction when arrivals stop, the final arm count is finite, and no arm lies on the 25 membership boundary. That conclusion does not apply to fixed-precision checkpoints. The general frontier under overlapping arrivals, automatic precision selection, and a matching converse for deferred maintenance remain open. The archived UCB-AA study also leaves a concrete empirical obligation: the repaired procedure must be compared under the same admission and retained-history rules before attributing a numerical gain to pre-elimination. Contextual information, delayed feedback, and post-arrival reward drift remain natural extensions of the original MAB-AA formulation. Data and code availability No original empirical or human-subject outcome data were collected. The original simulation configurations, endpoint records, source snapshots, and figures are preserved separately from the new reporting experiments. The release contains the 5,760 reporting runs, their fixed configuration, code, and checks.
